caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Botswana was long the textbook case of diamond-financed prudence: debt bottomed at 5.9% of GDP in 2007 and stayed near 20-25% through the 2010s, with large reserves in the Pula Fund. That era is ending. COVID pushed debt to 24.3% in 2020, and the 2024-25 diamond slump, as lab-grown stones and weak demand crushed De Beers sales, forced heavy borrowing: debt jumped to 32.8% in 2024 and a projected 38.6% in 2025, the series high. The government has drawn on reserves and issued domestic debt. Sustainability is not yet threatened, but the speed of the deterioration shows how a single-commodity fiscal model can unwind.
inflation_management: The Bank of Botswana has one of Africa's better inflation records, operating a crawling peg of the pula against a rand-and-SDR basket with a 3-6% objective range. Inflation spiked to 12.6% in 2008 on the global commodity boom and 11.6% in 2006, but the bank brought it down steadily to 1.9% in 2020, the series low. The 2022 shock pushed it back to 12.2%, and policy tightened in response; inflation fell to 5.1% in 2023 and 2.8% in both 2024 and 2025. The framework is credible and expectations are anchored, but with diamonds driving the economy, the real monetary risk is a terms-of-trade shock the exchange rate band cannot absorb.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis crushed diamond demand; debt jumped from 7.8% to 21.8% of GDP as the government spent to cushion the economy.
COVID-19: diamond sales collapsed; GDP in USD terms fell to $15.6bn.
Post-COVID diamond rebound took GDP to a series high of $20.3bn; inflation spiked to 12.2%.
October 30 election: Duma Boko's UDC coalition ended 58 years of BDP rule amid anger over unemployment and the diamond downturn; diamond revenues slumped, forcing a wider deficit.
Prolonged diamond market weakness pushed public debt to a projected 38.6% of GDP, a record, as the new government faced depleted buffers.

outlook_next_decade: The base case is a slow, painful adjustment: diamond revenues are unlikely to return to 2022 levels, forcing either spending cuts, new revenue sources, or a permanently higher debt path. Upside depends on diversification (tourism, financial services) and a diamond market recovery; downside is a fiscal crisis if borrowing continues while reserves erode. Uncertainty is moderate-to-high: the 2024 political turnover was peaceful, but the new government's economic program is untested.
